title: Isabella and the Pot of Basil

identifying_description: The painting was previously on loan to the Fine Arts Museums for the Truth and Beauty exhibition in 2018. This is an artist-made replica made of a full-scale version in the Laing Art Gallery in Newcastle from 1867. It measures 74 x 46 in. (187 x 116 cm). A significant difference between the two paintings is the inlay pattern on the prie-dieu.
web_text:
This picture portrays
a story from Giovanni Boccaccio’s book of tales the Decameron (1353), adapted by the English poet John Keats in 1818.
Having exhumed her dead lover’s body, Isabella conceals his head inside a
potted basil plant, watered with tears. His choice of this subject demonstrates
William Holman Hunt’s fascination with Medieval and early Renaissance culture,
but his treatment was also an exercise
in mourning. He and his wife, Fanny, had travelled to Florence in 1866; she
subsequently died there, and her memory served as his model for Isabella. He
was so attached to the composition that he painted it twice. The first version
is in the Laing Art Gallery in Newcastle, England.
